lines.text: 06May13
LOSS OF LIFE FOLLOWING MAN OVERBOARD FROM P/V QUEEN OF THE WEST
Analysis:
1. Policies: American Cruise Lines, Inc. implemented a number of policies designed to protect
crewmembers from harm onboard their vessels; namely, the "Crew in Quarters After Midnight, No
Smoking Onboard the Vessel, and No Alcohol Policies". Mr. Staples violated each of these policies on
the night of 06 August 2012 and early morning of 07 August 2012. Had Mr. Staples been in his quarters
by midnight, he would have not been in a position to fall overboard. Likewise, if he had abided by
company policy and gone to shore to smoke, instead of the stern, he probably would not have fallen
overboard. Had he refrained from drinking that night, he may have acted with better judgment than to
approach a dangerous area of the vessel.
Even though American Cruise Lines, Inc. made an effort to require crew to take certain safety
precautions, the implementation of a number of additional policies will help prevent this kind of accident
in the future. Namely, American Cruise Lines, Inc. has no formal, written lifejacket policy for their crews
stated that crewmembers were only told to wear lifejackets while working
to follow. Captain
lines for mooring and unmooring. Had a stronger safety culture with respect to lifejackets been in place
and enforced, Mr. Staples and his fellow crewmembers may have worn lifejackets out on deck in the early
morning of 07 August 2012. Additionally, a written policy detailing which crewmembers were
specifically granted access to the stern paddlewheel support arms (and for what reasons) will assist the
Captain in enforcing the lax “Authorized Personnel Only" policy. Inadequate enforcement of this
particular rule on the part of vessel management contributed to Mr. Staples (and other crewmembers)
believing that access to this particularly dangerous area of the vessel was permitted despite the posted
signage.
Safety policies are effected in order to thwart a passenger's or a crewmember's lapse of judgment.
Investigators visiting P/V QUEEN OF THE WEST saw definite areas where the implementation of
additional policies could save lives. But vessel managers must be willing and able to enforce policies
effectively. Reprimands and documentation of transgressors coupled with strong leadership and
continuous safety training will help vessel management ensure crew follow all company policies and will
ultimately lead to heightened safety.
2. Barricades and railings: Investígators also noted an insufficiency of physical barricades to prevent
crew and passengers alike from accessing the stern. "Employees Only" signs on main deck chains were
provided to restrict passenger access to the forward main deck areas only. But on two separate visits to
the vessel by investigators, they were not being used to deter passenger access. Most notably, there was a
complete absence of physical barriers to prevent the crew from approaching the stern, though ample
opportunity existed to put an effective barricade system in place. A simple chain (with a similar warning
sign as that used for passengers) attached to the bulkhead and stretched across the walkway in the
bottleneck area of the main deck immediately forward of the paddlewheel support arms would suffice as a
clear reminder to crew that the paddlewheel support arms are off-limits. Finally, investigators discovered
an eye-ring connection on the aftermost railing designe to provide a point of attachment for a grab line
or chain to protect personnel working on the paddlewheel support arms from accidentally falling directly
off the stern. The grab line or chain had never been placed into service, but vessel personnel stated they
could manufacture one very easily.
